Q: If clause doesn't work when getting result from an evaluation of a mongosh script A:

Colors in terminals are produced by ANSI escape codes. To echo true in yellow

echo -e "\e[93mtrue\e[0m"

true

Testing equality

ytrue="$(echo -ne "\e[93mtrue\e[0m")"
[ "$ytrue" = "true" ] || echo "$ytrue is not equal to 'true'"

true is not equal to 'true'

Try running the command as

docker exec -e NODE_DISABLE_COLORS=1 -it config1 mongosh --port 27019 --quiet --eval 'db.hello().isWritablePrimary'

Q: SonarQube Java path traversal attack A:

Before fixing anything, please understand the vulnerabilities. What this means is that when sonar (or any other similar tool) highlights a piece of code, don't try to get rid of the issue as quick as possible. Understand what the issue is. Do some research on the highlighted vulnerability.

This piece of code exposes for an attacker to get an understanding of the directory structure or get access to files which shouldn't be. normalize() is one of the step to fix this vulnerability, not the full fix. On how to approach a fix please read here

A sample fix too is given here. I hope that helps.

Q: Smoothly animating real-time GPS vehicle position with only 1 update/second, without adding lag A:

This is a UX problem. Accuracy is an inherent limit here since you posed the problem as future-sight. All you have left is: how do I make the user feel happy about the movement I'm showing? Note that this objective is different from making the movement be more accurate or feel more accurate.

At the very least you can make the assumption that real cars usually don't change acceleration tremendously from second to second and when they do, it's because something alarming has happened. You could consider a low-degree interpolation (e.g. treating acceleration calculated from the last step as constant) and aiming for different UX depending on the accuracy of this prediction.

Q: How do I make my Neovim open specific file instead of splash screen when I execute "nvim" in my shell? A:

Little different idea which can work with other programs too.

You can always create script with command /full/path/to/nvim /full/path/to/todo
and save it with name nvim (and make it executable).

If you will have this script in folder ~/bin and this folder will be as first on list PATH
then running command nvim you will run your script.

This way you may create scripts with other names which will start nvim with other files.

Or you may create alias instead of for script.
